\section{Reproducibility Details}
\label{app:reproducibility}

\paragraph{Fine-tuning configuration.}
All four fine-tuned models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on SciERC and DocRED) use identical LoRA hyperparameters: rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, no bias, targeting all attention and MLP projection layers (\texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, \texttt{o\_proj}, \texttt{gate\_proj}, \texttt{up\_proj}, \texttt{down\_proj}).
Training uses AdamW with learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, cosine schedule, warmup ratio $0.1$, effective batch size $16$, bf16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and completion-only loss for 3 epochs.
SciERC trains on 1,762 examples (260 dev) for 333 steps; DocRED trains on 3,053 examples (998 dev) for 573 steps.
Maximum sequence length is 2,048 (SciERC) and 4,096 (DocRED).
All runs use seed 42.

\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
Training runs on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (98\,GB video RAM (VRAM)).
SciERC fine-tuning takes approximately 11 minutes per model; DocRED takes approximately 1.5 hours.
Software versions: PyTorch 2.10, Transformers 4.57, PEFT 0.19, TRL 1.1, Accelerate 1.13.

\paragraph{Inference time.}
Inference timing is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:runtime} (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, same hardware as training).
S1 constrained decoding adds $+$13.1\% wall-clock overhead on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot greedy), lower on DocRED due to amortization over longer sequences; under LoRA fine-tuning, overhead is $+$10.0\% on SciERC.

\paragraph{Greedy decoding determinism.}
\label{app:greedy-determinism}
% exp_id: d067_seed_variance
All main results use greedy decoding (temperature$\,{=}\,$0, argmax token selection).
Argmax is deterministic: the random seed controls \texttt{torch.manual\_seed} for sampling and dropout, neither of which is active during greedy inference.
We verify this with three seeds (42, 123, 456) across two LoRA fine-tuned models on all 551 SciERC documents.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated on the same GPU, produce byte-identical outputs for both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
The residual variance in Table~\ref{tab:seed-variance} stems entirely from cross-hardware floating-point divergence: seed 42 was evaluated on a different server with a different CUDA driver version.
Even under this conservative upper bound, $\sigma(\text{E-F1}) \leq 0.16$\,pp, $\sigma(\text{R-F1}) \leq 0.43$\,pp, and $\sigma(\text{DR\%}) \leq 0.08$\,pp.
The constrained decoding DR\% reduction ($-$2.06\,pp for Qwen, $-$1.01\,pp for Llama) exceeds this variance by ${>}12\times$ (signal-to-noise ratio ${>}$\,12), confirming that observed improvements reflect genuine method effects rather than run-to-run noise.
We therefore report single-run results without error bars; bootstrap confidence intervals (10{,}000 iterations) are provided for F1 metrics.

\section{Use of AI Assistance}
We used Claude for coding, code drafting, debugging, and language polishing.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information extraction (IE)~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations} (DR): structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations are pervasive (15--18\% of triples under zero-shot decoding and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning) and correlate with schema restrictiveness rather than model scale.
At competitive quality, even low residual violation rates compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (CFGs) via XGrammar (JSON structure, vocabulary membership); the \emph{semantic layer} enforces type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to any autoregressive LM with logits access.
We validate across three model families, two RE datasets (up to 96 relation types), and event extraction (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}), with 70B-class supporting evidence (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
Composed with LoRA, greedy decoding reduces DR to near-zero ($\leq$\,0.21\%) at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency), with 97.6--100\% of removed triples confirmed as false positives; beam ($k{=}4$) achieves near-zero violations at ${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency.
DR enforcement converts irrecoverable ontology violations into cross-field type inconsistencies (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned), a severity downgrade amenable to post-hoc resolution.

OntoCoDec is orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework that reduces domain/range violations to near-zero ($\leq$\,0.21\%) without retraining or significant quality loss, showing that these type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}).
    \item An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only reduces DR by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, yet their composition achieves 94\%, because grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
    \item Supporting validation: scale-dependent interaction at 70B (semantic-only DR reduction grows from 24\% to 84\%; \S\ref{sec:70b-results}); beam $k{=}4$ achieves near-zero violations at 8B; event extraction generalization on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

These domain/range violations (DR) persist even after fine-tuning and cannot be resolved by grammar-constrained decoding, which lacks cross-field type awareness. 1	% Appendix B — Extended Discussion
2	% Contains discussion paragraphs moved from the main text during compression.
3	
4	\section{Extended Discussion}\label{app:discussion}
5	
6	%%% CF Dual Mechanism %%%
7	
8	\paragraph{CF Dual Mechanism.}
9	CF violations arise from two distinct mechanisms:
10	(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
11	The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.
12	(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type, which may differ from the entity's registered type.
13	
14	These mechanisms have sharply different model profiles.
15	Qwen3-8B triggers zero grammar-first fallbacks across all experiments, attributing 100\% of its CF violations to registry override.
16	Llama-3.1-8B, by contrast, triggers 5{,}882 fallbacks on SciERC (10.7 per document) and 57{,}825 on DocRED (63.8 per document), making grammar-first fallback the dominant CF source.
17	This asymmetry is consistent with the cross-model CF gap: Qwen achieves CF\,=\,2.57\% on DocRED vs.\ Llama's 12.02\%, despite both using identical constraint configurations.
18	The difference traces to Llama's less calibrated type predictions, which more frequently conflict with the semantic mask's valid set, triggering fallback.
19	
20	%%% Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage %%%
21	
22	\paragraph{Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage.}
23	\label{app:fallback-coverage}
24	The two-layer architecture produces two distinct fallback mechanisms with different semantic consequences.
25	\emph{Grammar-first fallback} occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations.
26	The token-level fallback rate (36.6\% on SciERC Llama) is inflated by continuation tokens of multi-token type names (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 BPE tokens); at semantically meaningful first-token positions, the rate is 0.04--5.7\% (zero-shot) and drops to $\leq$\,0.11\% under fine-tuning.
27	These events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.
28	\emph{Registry-consistent fallback} (4.5\%) occurs when the entity's registered type conflicts with domain/range constraints; the system defaults to the registered type for cross-triple consistency.
29	Together, these mechanisms produce the characteristic profile of composable constraint systems: residual DR traces to grammar-first fallback events, while CF violations arise from registry override events where per-relation enforcement assigns conflicting types.
30	
31	We define \emph{effective semantic constraint coverage} as $1 - f_{\text{gf}}$, where $f_{\text{gf}}$ is the grammar-first fallback rate.
32	On SciERC, Llama-3.1-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 36.6\%$ (6{,}237 of 17{,}024 mask calls), yielding 63.4\% effective coverage.
33	On DocRED, by contrast, Qwen3-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 0.08\%$ (46 of 54{,}859), yielding 99.9\% coverage.
34	The large discrepancy is primarily a tokenization artifact: SciERC entity types are multi-token (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 mask calls per type field), and continuation tokens necessarily conflict with the semantic mask, inflating the per-mask-call fallback rate.
35	DocRED types (\textsc{PER}, \textsc{ORG}, \textsc{LOC}, \textsc{TIME}, \textsc{NUM}, \textsc{MISC}) are all single-token, eliminating this inflation.
36	This metric directly quantifies the layer interaction (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): it measures the fraction of decoding steps where both constraint layers are jointly active, providing a fine-grained view beyond aggregate violation rates.
37	Qwen3-8B, with zero grammar-first fallbacks, achieves 100\% effective coverage on SciERC, consistent with its lower residual DR (0.93\% vs.\ Llama's 0.08\%).
38	
39	%%% Fallback Causal Tracing %%%
40	
41	\paragraph{Fallback Causal Tracing.}
42	\label{app:causal-tracing}
43	
44	To establish that grammar-first fallback is the \emph{sole} mechanism producing residual DR violations, we instrument the constraint processor to log, for each violation, whether the semantic mask was active ($S(t) \cap G(t) \neq \emptyset$) or bypassed via fallback ($S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$) at the type-bearing position.
45	Table~\ref{tab:causal-tracing} reports the results across four SciERC configurations.
46	
47	\begin{table}[t]
48	\centering
49	\small
50	\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
51	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
52	\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rrr@{}}
53	\toprule
54	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Setting} & \textbf{Fallback Rate} & \textbf{DR} & \textbf{From FB} \\
55	\midrule
56	Qwen3-8B  & FT S1 & 0/2256 (0\%)    & 0  & N/A \\
57	Qwen3-8B  & ZS S1 & 16/3458 (0.46\%) & 16 & 100\% \\
58	Llama-3.1-8B & FT S1 & 1/2162 (0.05\%) & 1  & 100\% \\
59	Llama-3.1-8B & ZS S1 & 1/2630 (0.04\%) & 1  & 100\% \\
60	\bottomrule
61	\end{tabular}}
62	\caption{Fallback causal tracing on SciERC (551 documents). Fallback Rate: type-bearing positions where $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ triggers grammar-first fallback. DR: residual domain/range violations. From FB: fraction of DR violations occurring at fallback positions. All violations occur exclusively at tail\_type positions (range constraints are tighter than domain constraints).}
63	\label{tab:causal-tracing}
64	\end{table}
65	
66	When the semantic mask is active, $\text{DR}_{\text{independent}} = 0$: the type constraint processor structurally prevents domain/range violations.
67	All 18 residual DR violations across four configurations occur exclusively at fallback positions, confirming that grammar-first fallback is a necessary condition for residual DR.
68	Fine-tuning reduces fallback to near-zero ($\leq$0.05\%), effectively eliminating the sole source of residual violations.
69	All fallback events occur at tail\_type positions, where $|\operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)|$ is smaller than $|\operatorname{dom}(r)|$, making the intersection $S(t) \cap G(t)$ more likely to be empty.
70	
71	%%% Enabling Dependency: Confound Analysis %%%
72	
73	\paragraph{Enabling Dependency: Confound Analysis.}
74	\label{app:enabling-confound}
75	
76	The scale-dependent layer interaction (\S\ref{sec:method}) shows that the semantic layer achieves only 24\% DR reduction without the grammar layer (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}).
77	A potential confound is that the semantic layer depends not only on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership but also on structural enforcement for positional awareness: the semantic layer identifies type-bearing positions by pattern-matching the decoded prefix against the JSON schema, which is reliable only when the grammar layer guarantees valid JSON structure.
78	Without grammar enforcement, malformed structure can cause the semantic layer to misidentify type-bearing positions, reducing effective coverage.
79	We quantify this via the semantic-only ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}, row~3): CF rises from 0.08\% to 2.71\%, indicating that 2.63\,pp of additional violations trace to structural ambiguity.
80	However, the dominant enabling mechanism remains vocabulary membership: the semantic layer's domain/range lookup requires $r_j \in \mathcal{R}$, which only the grammar layer ensures; without it, OOV relation names produce null constraint lookups.
81	The confound reinforces rather than undermines this interaction: both vocabulary and structural contributions of the grammar layer are prerequisites for effective semantic enforcement.
82	
83	%%% CF-DR Trade-off Analysis %%%
84	
85	\paragraph{CF-DR Trade-off Analysis.}

6	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
7	Grammar-constrained decoding restricts each token to a mask derived from a target grammar.

10	OntoCoDec fills this gap with a stateful semantic layer whose entity registry is populated dynamically during generation.
11	
12	\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
13	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, and others~\cite{guidex2025,josifoski2022genie,paolini2021tanl,cabot2021rebel,wang2023instructuie,qi2024adelie,fei2022lasuie,lu2022uie,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure via training-time internalization, learning schema preferences but without runtime guarantees: violations persist at 0.5--2\% even after fine-tuning~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.

20

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information extraction (IE)~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations} (DR): structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations are pervasive (15--18\% of triples under zero-shot decoding and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning) and correlate with schema restrictiveness rather than model scale.
At competitive quality, even low residual violation rates compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (CFGs) via XGrammar (JSON structure, vocabulary membership); the \emph{semantic layer} enforces type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to any autoregressive LM with logits access.
We validate across three model families, two RE datasets (up to 96 relation types), and event extraction (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}), with 70B-class supporting evidence (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
Composed with LoRA, greedy decoding reduces DR to near-zero ($\leq$\,0.21\%) at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency), with 97.6--100\% of removed triples confirmed as false positives; beam ($k{=}4$) achieves near-zero violations at ${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency.
DR enforcement converts irrecoverable ontology violations into cross-field type inconsistencies (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned), a severity downgrade amenable to post-hoc resolution.

OntoCoDec is orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework that reduces domain/range violations to near-zero ($\leq$\,0.21\%) without retraining or significant quality loss, showing that these type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}).
    \item An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only reduces DR by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, yet their composition achieves 94\%, because grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information extraction (IE)~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.

Violations are pervasive (15--18\% of triples under zero-shot decoding and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning) and correlate with schema restrictiveness rather than model scale.
At competitive quality, even low residual violation rates compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.

\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
\emph{Does grammar-constrained decoding alone resolve DR violations?}
Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} establishes that DR violations are pervasive (15--18\% across datasets) and that constraint layers interact non-additively: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%, the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}.
On DocRED (96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$), grammar-only \emph{increases} DR via \textit{latent violation surfacing}: forcing out-of-vocabulary (OOV)$\to$valid relation mapping exposes violations previously masked by vocabulary errors (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:docred-zs-ablation}).
Cross-model validation (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}) confirms DR drops of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with R-F1 improving in 5/6 settings; post-hoc filtering achieves DR${=}$0\% but at 14--74\% rejection rates.
The DR-to-CF conversion is a severity downgrade, not an error introduction (Figure~\ref{fig:violation-composition}): DR violations produce ontology-invalid triples that corrupt downstream knowledge graphs and cannot be fixed without re-extraction, while CF (individually valid triples with cross-triple type inconsistency) can be resolved via fine-tuning, beam search, or post-hoc reranking (TCR eliminates all CF with bounded DR regression; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
Zero-shot evaluation thus establishes violation prevalence and constraint interaction; fine-tuning demonstrates practical elimination.

%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning (expanded)
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
\emph{Does OntoCoDec retain value after fine-tuning?}
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 0.5--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}; full fine-tuning in Appendix~\ref{app:full-ft}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 (Bonferroni-corrected; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.69, {+}0.25]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream-impact}).
Under fine-tuning, grammar becomes a no-op ($\Delta$DR$<$0.2\,pp), making the semantic layer the sole DR defense (41--69\% on SciERC, 2--75\% on DocRED; Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}); three relations with $\kappa \geq 0.36$ retain DR, all eliminated by S1 (Appendix~\ref{app:lora-per-relation}).
CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (63.3\%; Appendices~\ref{app:cf-distribution},~\ref{app:cascade-analysis}); beam ($k{=}4$) achieves near-zero violations at 8B (R-F1 43--46; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

% CF analysis folded into composability paragraph above; details in Appendices~\ref{app:cf-distribution},~\ref{app:cascade-analysis}.
% Table 2 (composability) moved to section5_crossmodel_draft.tex for page 8 placement

%  (f) Downstream impact of DR elimination
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Downstream impact.}
\label{sec:downstream-impact}
Constraint removal affects only 0.24\% of gold triples; error analysis confirms only 0.2\% of false negatives were blocked by constraints (Appendices~\ref{app:lucky-violations},~\ref{app:error-analysis},~\ref{app:case-studies}).
The 36 residual DR violations across fine-tuned settings decompose into entity type errors (39\%), schema gaps (33\%), and relation/direction errors (28\%); the irreducible floor is $\sim$3 violations (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).

\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}

-\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via ILP; post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation but discards up to 74\% of predictions; grammar-only enforcement~\cite{geng2023gcd,boostcd2025} achieves only 3\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:constrained-baselines}).

+\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via integer linear programming (ILP); post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation but discards up to 74\% of predictions; grammar-only enforcement~\cite{geng2023gcd,boostcd2025} achieves only 3\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:constrained-baselines}).

EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} uses ASP; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} backtracks on violations; \citet{vukovic2024dialogue} combines ontology constraints with constrained chain-of-thought for dialogue RE.
These methods either operate post-hoc (discarding predictions) or require iterative refinement; OntoCoDec prevents violations during generation via forward-only stateful masking at $O(|V|)$ per step.

  "even low residual violation rates compound across thousands of documents into systematic
  knowledge graph corruption" — 这句把一个看似小问题（0.5-2% violation

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples: entity types that violate the schema's domain/range constraints for the predicted relation.
These domain/range violations (DR) persist even after fine-tuning and cannot be resolved by grammar-constrained decoding, which lacks cross-field type awareness.
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a two-layer constrained decoding framework that compiles IE ontologies into token-level masks: a grammar layer enforces structural validity; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime via stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.
The two layers interact non-additively: grammar-only reduces DR by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, yet their composition achieves 94\%.
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning across three model families and two relation extraction datasets (up to 96 relations), OntoCoDec reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% with minimal F1 impact ($\pm$0.3\,pp), converting irrecoverable type errors into correctable cross-field inconsistencies; beam search ($k{=}4$) achieves near-zero violations at ${\sim}$1.5$\times$ unconstrained latency.
Validation on a 70B model shows the semantic layer's independent effectiveness grows from 24\% to 84\% DR reduction with scale\footnote{Code and data are available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/schema_semantic_constrained_ie-FE20/}.}.
\end{abstract}
